title: Baseline specs: write down what the planner already does

blocks.text: 14.4.1 Baseline Specs: Write Down What the Planner Already Does

GridCap's capital planner works. It chooses which projects to start, and in which year, within a yearly budget, and the planners use it every cycle. Now they have a queue of changes for it: a regional share, must-do overrides, carry-over, and an old cap to retire. Before the first one, the team lead writes this:

**Request 1.** Before we touch any rule, write down what the planner does today, in words the planners can read and sign and in a form the tests can check. From now on, a rule changes only after its change is written and agreed. And something has to check that the written rules are well formed, or they will rot like every wiki page before them.

This module takes that request, and the five changes after it, through **Spec-Driven Development** (SDD): the spec says what the system must do, and it is written and agreed before the code that does it. The workflow is **OpenSpec** `2.0.0`, an open-source spec workflow. The project lives in complete snapshots: `steps/00` is the planner before this lesson, `steps/01` the project after it. The portfolios are invented, made by a seeded generator in the project (GridCap is fictional).
The Planner Works, but Its Rules Live Only in Its Code and Six Tests

The planner, snapshot `steps/00`, is a package of five modules: `portfolio.py` holds the project records and the generator, `request.py` what the planners ask for, `model.py` the model, `plan.py` the solve, and `report.py` what a plan spends. A project carries an id, a region (`north`, `plains` or `coast`), a cost in $k paid in the year it starts, a value in $k, and the earliest and latest years it may start. `baseline.py` plans 40 invented projects over 2027 to 2031:

40 fictional projects, $3,000k a year for 2027-2031: 15 started, value $18,616k (OPTIMAL)
starts per year: 2027 3, 2028 3, 2029 3, 2030 3, 2031 3

The model is a 0-1 model with start-time variables (lesson 6.4.1), solved with CP-SAT, the OR-Tools solver for integer models (lesson 4.4.1). CP-SAT takes integer data only, which suits GridCap: every cost, value and budget is a whole number of $k.
The Model
The planner's model, as `steps/00` builds it. This lesson does not change it; it writes down what it does.
**Sets.** $`P`$, the projects; $`Y`$, the plan years, 2027 onward; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$, the plan years from project $`i`$'s earliest to its latest start year.

**Parameters.** $`c_i`$, the cost of project $`i`$ ($k), paid in its start year; $`v_i`$, its value ($k); $`B`$, the budget of each plan year ($k); $`K`$, the most projects that may start in one year (3 unless the request sets another).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0,1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$. A year outside $`T_i`$ has no variable, so no start there is possible.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} v_i \, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.** With $`\text{spend}_y = \sum_{i \in P :\, y \in T_i} c_i \, x_{i,y}`$, what the plan spends in year $`y`$:

In the code the rows are named `once_P007`, `budget_2029` and `starts_2029`, and the variables `x_P007_2029`. The six tests of `steps/00` each check one rule on a hand-made portfolio of one to five projects, by fixing a plan and asking the model whether it allows it (lesson 12.3.1), or by comparing the plan with the best plan found by trying every one.
What the planners cannot do is read any of this. The rules are rows and test functions, and the one place that says "the cap is three starts a year" is a default argument in `request.py`.
OpenSpec Keeps the Living Specs and the Proposed Changes Apart
OpenSpec puts everything in one folder, `openspec/`, with two parts:

rows: the **living specs**: how the system behaves now, one file per capability
one **change** in progress: `proposal.md` (why, and what changes), `tasks.md` (the checklist), an optional `design.md` (how), and `specs/<capability>/spec.md`, the **spec deltas**
each finished change, kept whole for its history

blocks.text: A **capability** is one area of behaviour with a spec of its own; this project will have two. A **spec delta** says only what a change does to a living spec: which requirements it adds, modifies, removes or renames. A change goes through four moves:

items: **Propose.** Write the change folder: the proposal, the deltas, the tasks.
**Review and validate.** The owners read the proposal and the deltas before any code, and `openspec validate` checks their format.
**Apply.** Work through the tasks, checking each off.

**Archive.** `openspec archive` merges the deltas into the living specs and moves the change to `changes/archive/`, so the living specs describe the new behaviour and the next change starts from them.

blocks.text: The OpenSpec CLI is an npm package that needs Node.js. The course's runner image carries both, Node.js 24.21.0 and OpenSpec 2.0.0 with its telemetry off, and the program `openspec_cli.py` runs the real CLI on a temporary copy of every step, so the repository's own files never change:

$ openspec --version
2.0.0
(exit 0)

These are the commands for this lesson's change. `openspec_cli.py` runs the last three; the first three stay read-along, because the snapshots already hold the folders they would create. `--tools none` sets up the folder without installing commands for any editor tool.

openspec init --tools none                       # creates openspec/  (read-along)
openspec new change add-baseline-specs           # creates openspec/changes/add-baseline-specs/  (read-along)
openspec show add-baseline-specs                 # prints the change  (read-along)
openspec validate --all --strict                 # checks every change and living spec
openspec list                                    # active changes; --specs lists the living specs
openspec archive add-baseline-specs --yes        # merges the deltas and archives the change
Validation names `--all` (or one item). With neither, and no terminal to ask in, the CLI checks nothing and exits 1:

$ openspec validate --strict
Nothing to validate. Try one of:
  openspec validate --all
  openspec validate --changes
  openspec validate --specs
  openspec validate <item-name>
Or run in an interactive terminal.
(exit 1)

The project also ships `specs_check.py`, a Python checker of about 300 lines, so that each snapshot checks its own specs in its tests with Python alone. It mirrors the format rules of `openspec validate --strict` that these specs need, and the archive merge, as read in OpenSpec's source. It is not the OpenSpec CLI, and it says so on its first line of output. Its commands are `python3 specs_check.py list`, `validate --strict` and `archive <change-id> --date <date>`. The pages show its output and the real CLI's side by side.

OpenSpec's advice for an existing project is to write specs only for what you are about to change, and let them grow change by change, rather than back-fill a spec of everything. Every change in this module touches the planning rules, so this first change specifies those rules and nothing else of the planner: not the generator, not the report's layout.
A Requirement States One Behaviour With SHALL or MUST; a Scenario Says When and Then

A spec has a `## Purpose` and a `## Requirements` section. Each requirement is a `### Requirement:` heading with its text under it, and the text carries **SHALL** or **MUST**, the keywords of RFC 2119 for an absolute requirement (**SHOULD** and **MAY** mark weaker ones). Under each requirement come its **scenarios**: `#### Scenario:` headings, each with steps as bullets, **GIVEN** a starting state, **WHEN** something happens, **THEN** the outcome, and **AND** to continue a step.

The change's delta for the planner, `specs/capital-plan/spec.md`, adds five requirements. Because the capability is new, the delta opens with the `## Purpose` the living spec will get, then an `## ADDED Requirements` section:
<!-- snapshot: steps/01/openspec/changes/archive/2026-11-02-add-baseline-specs/specs/capital-plan/spec.md -->

## Purpose
Which of GridCap's capital projects the planner starts, and in which year, within the planners'
budget and rules. GridCap is a fictional utility.

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Yearly budget
The planner SHALL keep what the plan spends in each plan year within the yearly budget, counting
each project's whole cost in the year it starts.

#### Scenario: Spending up to the budget is allowed
- **GIVEN** a budget of $1,000k a year
- **WHEN** a plan starts a $600k project and a $400k project in 2027
- **THEN** the plan is allowed

#### Scenario: Spending over the budget is refused
- **GIVEN** a budget of $1,000k a year
- **WHEN** a plan starts a $600k project and a $410k project in 2027
- **THEN** the plan is refused

The other four requirements follow the same shape: one start per project, the start window, the yearly start cap, and the most valuable plan. Read the spec for what it leaves out. It names no variable, no row and no solver. OpenSpec's guide calls a spec a behaviour contract: what anyone can observe and check, with internal names and library choices left to the design and the code. A planner can sign "the cap is 3 when the request does not set one"; nobody signs $`K`$.
The scenarios were not invented: each one is an existing test, written as words. The test names already said what each test checks, so each scenario took its test's name:

capital-plan scenarios, and the test of steps/00 each one names:
  Spending up to the budget is allowed             test_spending_up_to_the_budget_is_allowed (in steps/00)
  Spending over the budget is refused              test_spending_over_the_budget_is_refused (in steps/00)
  A project started twice is refused               test_a_project_started_twice_is_refused (in steps/00)
  A start outside the window is refused            test_a_start_outside_the_window_is_refused (in steps/00)
  More starts than the cap are refused             test_more_starts_than_the_cap_are_refused (in steps/00)
  The plan has the greatest value within the rules test_the_plan_has_the_greatest_value_within_the_rules (in steps/00)

That naming is this project's own convention: a scenario's test is `test_` and the scenario's name in lower case, with each run of other characters as one underscore. OpenSpec does not require it. The project keeps it for the rest of the module, and the last lesson checks it.
The Checker Applies the Format Rules That Strict Validation Applies

The change's second delta, `specs/spec-checks/spec.md`, specifies the checker itself, as a second capability: the format rules it applies, each with its scenarios. They are the rules OpenSpec's validator applies to every requirement, read in its source (`src/core/validation/validator.ts` at `v2.0.0`):

rows: a requirement has text under its header
the text has SHALL or MUST (in the text, not only the header)
a requirement has a scenario with steps under it
a scenario has a WHEN or GIVEN step and a THEN step
a living spec has `## Purpose` and `## Requirements`
the Purpose has at least 50 characters
`--strict` fails on any warning, plain validation on errors only

blocks.text: A scenario heading with nothing under it does not count as a scenario, in either. The keyword rule reads the text: a header such as `### Requirement: The planner SHALL keep the budget` with no keyword in the text under it still gets the warning, because OpenSpec's validator reads the keyword on the lines under the header.
The checker of `steps/00` can already read a spec into requirements and scenarios, but its `check_requirement` is a stub that fails every requirement. This change writes it:

--- 00/specs_check.py
+++ 01/specs_check.py
@@
 def check_requirement(req: Requirement, where: str) -> list[Issue]:
-    """The rules every requirement keeps. (Stub: the next lesson writes them; until then none passes.)"""
-    return [Issue("ERROR", where, f'requirement "{req.name}" has not been checked')]
+    """The rules every requirement keeps, in a living spec and in an ADDED or MODIFIED delta."""
+    issues = []
+    if not req.text:
+        issues.append(Issue("ERROR", where, f'requirement "{req.name}" has no text under its header'))
+    elif not KEYWORD.search(req.text):
+        issues.append(Issue("WARNING", where, f'requirement "{req.name}" should contain SHALL or MUST in its text'))
+    scenarios = {name: body for name, body in req.scenarios.items() if body}
+    if not scenarios:
+        issues.append(Issue("ERROR", where, f'requirement "{req.name}" must include at least one scenario'))

`KEYWORD` matches SHALL or MUST as whole upper-case words. The rest of the function is the last rule of the table, and it is yours to write in the practice: for each scenario with a body, a WARNING `scenario "<name>" is missing <what>` when it has no WHEN or GIVEN step (`a WHEN or GIVEN step`) or no THEN step (`a THEN step`), both joined by ` and ` when both are missing, and then the list of issues. `has_steps(body)` is already in the checker: it returns two booleans, whether the body has a trigger step and whether it has an outcome step, and it finds a step keyword in bold in any case (`**When**`) or bare in upper case (`WHEN`), as OpenSpec's reader does. To see the rules work, `baseline.py` plants faults in a copy of the capital-plan delta: first the keyword taken out of one requirement and the THEN step out of one scenario, then also every step out of the Start window requirement's only scenario:

-- two faults
WARNING add-baseline-specs/specs/capital-plan/spec.md: requirement "One start per project" should contain SHALL or MUST in its text
WARNING add-baseline-specs/specs/capital-plan/spec.md: scenario "The plan has the greatest value within the rules" is missing a THEN step
plain validation passes; strict validation fails
-- three faults
WARNING add-baseline-specs/specs/capital-plan/spec.md: requirement "One start per project" should contain SHALL or MUST in its text
ERROR   add-baseline-specs/specs/capital-plan/spec.md: requirement "Start window" must include at least one scenario
WARNING add-baseline-specs/specs/capital-plan/spec.md: scenario "The plan has the greatest value within the rules" is missing a THEN step
plain validation fails; strict validation fails
The real CLI, run by `openspec_cli.py` on the same two copies of the change, reports the same issues at the same levels, in the same order, and reaches the same verdicts: exit 0 is a pass.

✓ change/add-baseline-specs
Totals: 1 passed, 0 failed (1 items)

(exit 0)

(exit 1)
== add-baseline-specs with three faults
$ openspec validate --all
Totals: 0 passed, 1 failed (1 items)
Details: openspec validate add-baseline-specs --type change
✗ change/add-baseline-specs
  ⚠ [WARNING] capital-plan/spec.md: ADDED "One start per project" should contain SHALL or MUST (RFC 2119 best practice for English specs)
  ✗ [ERROR] capital-plan/spec.md: ADDED "Start window" must include at least one scenario (a scenario header with no body under it does not count; add its steps, e.g. "- **WHEN** ..." and "- **THEN** ...")
  ⚠ [WARNING] capital-plan/spec.md: ADDED "Most valuable plan": scenario "The plan has the greatest value within the rules" is missing a THEN step. A scenario needs a trigger and an outcome, e.g. "- **WHEN** an invoice is voided" and "- **THEN** a credit note is issued".
(exit 1)
Only the wording differs: the CLI names the file from the capability folder, says which delta section the requirement is in (`ADDED`), and adds a hint to each message.

Two warnings pass plain validation and fail strict validation. That is why the project validates with `--strict`: a requirement without SHALL is a sentence nobody can hold the planner to, and a scenario without THEN asserts nothing, so neither should ever reach the living specs.
The Proposal Says Why; the Tasks Put Tests Before Code
OpenSpec's proposal template has four parts: **Why**, **What Changes**, **Capabilities** (new and modified, each a folder under `specs/`) and **Impact**. This change's proposal:
<!-- snapshot: steps/01/openspec/changes/archive/2026-11-02-add-baseline-specs/proposal.md -->

## Why
The planner's rules live only in its code and in six tests. Before the planners change a rule (a
regional share is next), the team needs today's rules written as requirements a planner can read
and a test can check, and a checker that keeps those specs in OpenSpec's format.

## What Changes
- Specify the planner as it is today: the yearly budget, one start per project, start windows, the
  yearly start cap and the most valuable plan. The planner's behaviour does not change.
- Specify the rules the checker applies to requirements and scenarios, and write them in
  specs_check.py.

The tasks are a checklist in numbered groups, `## 1.` then `- [ ] 1.1 ...`, and each box is ticked as the task is done. OpenSpec's guide asks that each group carry its own tests rather than leave them to a last group; this project goes one step further and puts the tests before the code they check:
<!-- snapshot: steps/01/openspec/changes/archive/2026-11-02-add-baseline-specs/tasks.md -->

## 1. Specs
- [x] 1.1 Write the capital-plan delta: one requirement per rule the code keeps, one scenario per existing test
- [x] 1.2 Write the spec-checks delta: the rules check_requirement will apply

## 2. Tests from the scenarios
- [x] 2.1 Keep the six planner tests; rename none, since each is already named after its scenario
- [x] 2.2 Write tests/test_spec_checks.py, one test per spec-checks scenario, and see each fail on the stub

## 3. Code
- [x] 3.1 Write check_requirement in specs_check.py
- [x] 3.2 Run the tests and `specs_check.py validate --strict`; both pass

## 4. Archive
- [x] 4.1 Archive the change, so the two deltas become the living specs
Seven tasks in four groups: the specs first, then the tests, then the code, then the archive.
Each Scenario Becomes a Test, and Each Test Fails Before the Code Exists
Each spec-checks scenario becomes one test, named after it, on a small spec written in the test:
<!-- snapshot: steps/01/tests/test_spec_checks.py -->

def test_a_keyword_only_in_the_header_does_not_count():
    name = "The planner SHALL keep the budget"
    issues = check_spec(spec(f"### Requirement: {name}\nSpending stays within it.\n\n" + FITS), "demo")
    assert issues == [Issue("WARNING", "demo", f'requirement "{name}" should contain SHALL or MUST in its text')]

A test that has never failed has not shown that it tests anything. The stub returns a wrong answer instead of raising, so each failure is the assertion the scenario predicts, not an import error. The last test, "These specs pass strict validation", runs the checker on the project's own `openspec/` folder, so from now on a malformed spec fails the test suite.
Validate, Then Archive: the Deltas Become the Living Specs
With the change proposed and the code still that of `steps/00`, strict validation fails on every requirement, because the stub checks none. With the change's code, it passes:

== validate --strict, the change proposed, with the checker of steps/01
valid   change add-baseline-specs
strict: 0 item(s) failed
The real CLI validates the same proposed change, and lists it; `specs_check.py list` on the same folder follows:

== add-baseline-specs, proposed on steps/00
$ openspec validate --all --strict
✓ change/add-baseline-specs
Totals: 1 passed, 0 failed (1 items)
(exit 0)
$ openspec list
Changes:
  add-baseline-specs     ✓ Complete    just now
(exit 0)
-- specs_check.py list, the same folder, with the checker of steps/01
Changes:
  add-baseline-specs           7/7 tasks
Specs:

Archiving merges each delta into its living spec and moves the change folder. Both capabilities are new, so archive creates both specs, each with the delta's Purpose and a `# <capability> Specification` title, as OpenSpec's archive writes it:

The verdicts and the files agree. Two things differ, and both are in how the tools report:

items: **The archive's date.** The CLI names the archive folder after the day it runs, which the program prints as `<today>`; `specs_check.py archive` takes the date with `--date`, which is how the snapshots keep `2026-11-02`. With the date set aside, every file under `openspec/` is the same.

**The list.** `openspec list` shows only the changes (`openspec list --specs` shows the living specs), writes `✓ Complete` when every task is ticked, and adds how long ago the change last changed (`just now`, since the program stamps its copy with the time it runs). `specs_check.py list` shows the changes and the specs together, and counts the tasks, here `7/7 tasks`.

blocks.text: `main.py` now also checks the specs on every run, and the step's report gains a line:

--- 00/main.py
+++ 01/main.py
@@
 from __future__ import annotations
 
+from pathlib import Path
+
 from capplan.plan import plan
@@
 from capplan.request import Request
+from specs_check import passes, requirements, sections, validate
@@
         print(f"  {year}: {len(starts)} starts, ${spend:,}k  {' '.join(starts)}")
+    root = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
+    specs = sorted((root / "openspec" / "specs").glob("*/spec.md"))
+    reqs = [r for spec in specs for r in requirements(dict(sections(spec.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))["Requirements"])]
+    verdict = "passed" if all(passes(issues) for issues in validate(root).values()) else "FAILED"
+    print(f"openspec: {len(specs)} specs, {len(reqs)} requirements, "
+          f"{sum(len(r.scenarios) for r in reqs)} scenarios; strict validation {verdict}")
What the Step Did to the Code

step  planner lines  checker lines  tests  requirements  scenarios  most branching planner function
00               98            296      6             0          0  model.build (5)
01              101            309     14            10         14  model.build (5)

The planner gained 3 lines, a stub field and a stub function for the next lesson, and no behaviour. The checker gained 13. The real growth is in what the project knows about itself: 10 requirements and 14 scenarios, each a sentence a planner can read, and 8 new tests that keep the specs well formed.

**Practice.** This lesson's project practice starts from `steps/00`, the whole package, with the specs and tests of `steps/01`. It is graded by those tests and by a check that `main.py` prints `steps/01/expected/report.txt`, the tiny portfolio's plan followed by the line about the specs.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Summary

items: **Specs come before changes.** The first change writes down what the planner already does, from its tests, before any rule changes.
**OpenSpec keeps living specs apart from proposed changes.** A change is a folder with a proposal, tasks, an optional design, and spec deltas; archive merges the deltas and keeps the folder.
**A requirement states one behaviour with SHALL or MUST in its text; each scenario has WHEN (or GIVEN) and THEN.** A spec names no variable, row or solver.
**Strict validation fails on warnings too.** A requirement without SHALL and a scenario without THEN pass plain validation and fail strict validation.

**`specs_check.py` mirrors the rules; it is not the OpenSpec CLI.** The course image now runs the real CLI too, and on this change the two agree on every verdict and every file; they differ in the archive's date and in what `list` shows.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: `### Requirement: <name>`, then text with SHALL or MUST

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [CP-SAT Solver (OR-Tools docs)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver) (CP-SAT takes integer data, and the statuses `OPTIMAL`, `FEASIBLE` and `INFEASIBLE` the planner reads); [OpenSpec README, `v2.0.0`](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/v2.0.0/README.md) (what OpenSpec is, its MIT license, and installing it with npm on Node.js `22.12.0` or later); [Concepts (OpenSpec docs, `v2.0.0`)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/v2.0.0/docs/concepts.md) (specs and changes, the spec format, a spec as a behaviour contract, proposal, design, tasks, archive); [Using OpenSpec in an existing project (OpenSpec docs, `v2.0.0`)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/v2.0.0/docs/existing-projects.md) (specify only what you are about to change); [CLI reference (OpenSpec docs, `v2.0.0`)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/v2.0.0/docs/cli.md) (`init --tools none`, `new change`, `list`, `show`, `validate --strict`, `archive --yes`); [`validator.ts` (OpenSpec source, `v2.0.0`)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/v2.0.0/src/core/validation/validator.ts) and [`requirement-text.ts` (OpenSpec source, `v2.0.0`)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/blob/v2.0.0/src/core/parsers/requirement-text.ts) (the rules `specs_check.py` mirrors, and how a step keyword is read); [spec-driven templates (OpenSpec source, `v2.0.0`)](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/tree/v2.0.0/schemas/spec-driven/templates) (the proposal, spec, design and tasks templates). Lessons 4.4.1 (CP-SAT variables and constraints), 6.4.1 (start-time variables) and 12.3.1 (testing one constraint at a time) are the course's background for the planner.
Challenges

items: The planners say the cap is "three a year, but four in 2031, the year the new crew starts". Write the requirement's new text and one scenario, and say whether it is still one behaviour.
Write a scenario for "Most valuable plan" that a planner could check by hand on two projects, without trying every plan.
A colleague proposes to specify the report's layout too, line by line. Using OpenSpec's advice for existing projects, argue for or against doing it in this change.

blocks.text: Design Note: The Scenarios Come From the Tests, Not the Other Way Round

A baseline can be written from the code, by reading what the rows do, or from the tests. This one was written from the tests, for two reasons. A test is the closest thing to a scenario the project already had: a starting state, an action and an outcome. And a rule that no test checked would have become a scenario no test checks, which is exactly the gap a spec should expose rather than hide. The cost is that a baseline written this way is only as complete as the tests were. Here they covered every row, and the last lesson of the module adds the check that keeps it so.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**baseline.py.** Plans 40 invented projects with `steps/00`, maps each scenario to its test, validates the proposed change with the stub and with the real checker, plants faults in the delta, archives the change, and runs the step's tests before and after (*every section*). *Try:* Change "SHALL" to "should" in one requirement of the planted copy. Predict whether plain validation passes, then run it.

**openspec_cli.py.** Runs the real OpenSpec CLI, with subprocess and a fixed list of arguments, on a temporary copy of every snapshot and of every change proposed on the snapshot before it: `--version`, `validate --all --strict`, `list --specs`, `list` and `archive <id> --yes`, then compares what archive wrote with the snapshot. It also validates this lesson's planted faults (*the OpenSpec folder, the checker, validate and archive*). *Try:* Remove `--all` from `VALIDATE`. Predict the exit status of every validation, then run it.
